docs.title: Solar Tracker Tilt-Sensing System
docs.text:
A sub-$10 tilt sensor for solar tracker rows that needs no power on the follower row.

Sponsored by ARRAY Technologies, a solar tracker manufacturer.

The problem How it works

docs.title: What we're building
docs.text:
Single-axis solar trackers turn rows of panels to follow the sun. One drive row carries the motor, and the follower rows are linked to it mechanically. If a follower row drifts out of line with the drive row, the farm loses energy and the row can be damaged.

Our device measures the follower row's tilt relative to the drive row and reports it to the ARRAY controller over RS-485. Everything powered sits on the drive row. The follower row only carries a passive reflector.

  • The Problem

    Why follower-row drift matters and the sponsor's hard constraints.

  • Our Solution

    Infrared pulses, a passive reflector and a differential photodiode pair.

  • Design Decisions

    How we got from five concepts to one, and what changed since.

  • Technology

    Emitter, detector, electronics and power budget.

  • Budget & Unit Cost

    The $540 team budget and the per-unit cost to ARRAY.

  • Milestones

    Eleven milestones from design to handoff on May 1, 2027.

What the estimate covers

  • Uses the bare MCU chip, not the module.
  • Field illuminator supplied by ARRAY.
  • Assumes ~100 units. At 5-unit prototype quantities the same board costs 3–4× more per unit.

We're confirming with ARRAY whether the under-$10 target means electronics only or the whole unit, enclosure included.

docs.title: Nov 3, 2026: Concept 5 selected
docs.text:
At the sponsor meeting, ARRAY endorsed a hybrid IR approach: emitter and detector on the drive row, passive reflector on the follower row.

  • Magnetic encoder rejected because running wire between rows costs too much.
  • Ultrasonic rejected because it needs power on the follower row.
  • Both reflector variants approved for prototyping: flat square and shaped.
  • Action items: source IR emitters that can be purchased off the shelf, target IP66 sealing, prefer UL / cULus listed parts.

docs.title: Nov 16–17, 2026: Plan rebuilt on 11 milestones
docs.text: Following faculty feedback, the team rebuilt the project plan from 9 to 11 milestones. The board from WBS Day (Nov 16) is the source of truth. See Milestones.

docs.title: Nov 19, 2026: Sensor range revision
docs.text:
Finding

The bare SFH 4547 emitter and BPW34 detector pair is only good for about 3–4 m, but rows are 6–8 m apart. The round-trip return in sunlight is the biggest design risk.

Decision:

  • Keep the bare pair for bench work proving the angle-measurement principle.
  • Add one Benewake TFmini Plus LiDAR module (~$52) to test the full 6–8 m range in the field.
  • The sensor budget line rose from about $100 to about $150, and the total team budget from \(490 to **\)540**.

docs.title: Nov 23, 2026: Budget settled
docs.text: The team budget was finalized at **\(540**. The under-\)10 per-unit cost to ARRAY covers the sensing-node electronics at about 100 units. The enclosure and field illuminator are costed separately, and we're confirming that scope with ARRAY. See Budget & Unit Cost.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Single-axis solar trackers rotate rows of panels to follow the sun across the sky. In a typical layout, one drive row carries the motor, and several follower rows are mechanically linked to it so they turn together.

If a follower row's tilt drifts out of alignment with the drive row:

  • the farm produces less energy, because those panels no longer face the sun correctly, and
  • the row can be mechanically damaged.

ARRAY Technologies needs a low-cost way to measure the follower row's tilt angle relative to the drive row and report it to the ARRAY controller.

docs.title: Sponsor constraints
docs.text:
No power on the follower row

Power exists only on the drive (main) row. Anything placed on the follower row has to work without electricity.

Under $10 per unit

The final device cost to ARRAY has to stay under $10 per unit. See Budget & Unit Cost for what that figure covers.

6–8 m between rows

The sensor has to work across the full gap between rows in the field.

Outdoors, all year

Direct sunlight, heat up to a +60 °C target, and weather. The enclosure needs to be sealed (IP66 target).

±1° accuracy, RS-485 output

Tilt must be measured to within ±1° and reported to the ARRAY controller over RS-485.

docs.title: Our Solution: Concept 5
docs.text:
An infrared emitter and detector on the drive row, and a passive reflector on the follower row. The follower row needs no electronics and no power.

flowchart TB
    subgraph DR["Drive row (powered, 24 V)"]
        E["IR emitter<br/>940 nm, pulsed"]
        D["Differential photodiode pair"]
        M["MCU<br/>calibration curve"]
        T["RS-485 transceiver"]
    end
    subgraph FR["Follower row (0 W)"]
        R["Passive reflector"]
    end
    C["ARRAY controller"]

    E -- "IR pulses across 6–8 m" --> R
    R -- "Reflected spot" --> D
    D --> M --> T -- "Tilt angle" --> C

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Emit. The drive-row unit fires modulated 940 nm infrared pulses across the 6–8 m gap to the follower row.
  2. Reflect. A passive reflector mounted on the follower row sends the light back. It needs no power or electronics.
  3. Detect. A differential pair of photodiodes on the drive row reads where the returned spot lands. As the follower row tilts, the spot moves, and the ratio between the two detectors changes.
  4. Convert. The MCU maps that ratio to a tilt angle using a calibration curve built against a reference inclinometer.
  5. Report. The drive-row unit sends the tilt angle to the ARRAY controller over RS-485.

The reflected light is the follower row's only output

Its tilt is encoded in where the light comes back.

docs.title: Why this approach
docs.text:
• It meets the zero-power constraint directly. All powered parts sit on the drive row.
  • There's no wiring between rows. Cable between rows was the main cost of the magnetic-encoder concept.
  • Parts are cheap at volume. The emitter and both detectors cost under $2 together at about 100 units.

docs.title: Reflector variants
docs.text:
The sponsor approved prototyping two reflector shapes, and we'll compare them on the bench:

  • a flat square reflector
  • a shaped reflector

docs.title: Biggest risk: range
docs.text: The bare emitter and detector pair is a 3–4 m class link, but rows sit 6–8 m apart. Getting a usable return signal across that distance in full sunlight is the #1 design risk. See the Nov 19 decision for how we're testing it.

docs.title: The optical link
docs.text:
Emitter: SFH 4547Detector: BPW34Range test: TFmini PlusField illuminator

ams OSRAM SFH 4547, a 940 nm infrared LED mounted on the drive row.

  • 50 mW/sr radiant intensity
  • $0.86 each in small quantities, $0.44 at 100
  • Pulses at 100 mA, which is more than an MCU pin can supply, so it needs an emitter-driver MOSFET

Vishay BPW34, a PIN photodiode used as a differential pair.

  • 950 nm peak sensitivity, ±65° acceptance angle
  • 100 ns response, fast enough for pulse timing
  • $1.37 each in small quantities, $0.72 at 100
  • Photocurrent is read through a transimpedance amplifier (TIA)

Note

We aren't using the SFH 309 phototransistor because it's end of life.

Benewake TFmini Plus, a complete LiDAR module with its own emitter and detector.

  • 0.1–12 m range, IP65
  • ~$52
  • It measures distance, not angle, so it's used only to validate range across the 6–8 m gap. It isn't part of the product.

For field use, ARRAY supplies the illuminator. It isn't part of the team budget.

  • Primary: Bosch IIR-50940-SR: 940 nm, IP66, cULus, 12–32 V DC, 13 W, rated −50 to +50 °C
  • Alternate: Pelco IR940M-60
  • These illuminators stay on continuously with a photocell, so our timing channel uses pulse modulation.
  • We're checking the +50 °C rating against our +60 °C target with ARRAY.

docs.title: Camera Concept
docs.text:
Alternative concept under study

This is an alternative to Concept 5 that the team is evaluating. It is not the selected design. Idea and simulation by Lakshanand Sugumar.

A small camera on the drive row watches two colored markers on the follower row. As the follower row tilts, the markers move in the image. After a one-time teaching sweep against a reference inclinometer, the camera reads the follower's tilt angle directly. The follower row still needs no power.

flowchart TB
    subgraph DR["Drive row (powered, 24 V)"]
        C["Camera on a fixed post<br/>640 × 480, 60° view"]
        M["MCU<br/>color subtraction + taught table"]
        T["RS-485"]
    end
    subgraph FR["Follower row (0 W)"]
        P["Pink marker<br/>near edge"]
        Y["Yellow marker<br/>far edge"]
    end
    P -. "seen by" .-> C
    Y -. "seen by" .-> C
    C --> M --> T --> CTRL["ARRAY controller"]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. See. A camera on a fixed post at the drive row looks across the 6–8 m gap at the follower row.
  2. Isolate the markers with color subtraction. For every pixel, yellow score = min(R, G) − B and pink score = min(R, B) − G. Sand, steel, sky and the dark solar cells all score near zero, so only the markers stand out.
  3. Find each marker's center. The weighted center of each color blob gives its position to a fraction of a pixel.
  4. Teach. During on-site calibration, the follower row is swept from −60° to +60° next to a reference inclinometer. At each 2° step the camera records the gap between the yellow and pink markers in the image, and the pink marker's own height.
  5. Measure. In service, the camera looks up the current marker positions in the taught table to get the tilt angle, then reports it over RS-485.

docs.title: Why two markers on opposite edges
docs.text:
• Wind on the camera post cancels out. If the post sways, both markers shift together in the image, so the gap between them stays the same.
  • The colors give the direction. Whichever marker sits higher tells you which way the row tilted.
  • The near marker is never hidden. When the panel is almost edge-on to the camera, the module partly hides the far marker. The near pink marker stays visible and picks the correct reading. The simulation found this effect; see Results.
  • They're offset 1 m along the row, so the two markers never overlap in the image.

docs.title: Cost Under $10
docs.text:
The whole unit, including camera, 3D-printed shell and mounting hardware, has to cost under $10. A build from off-the-shelf modules with no custom PCB gets there.

Estimates at about 100 units. Prices are not quotes.

Item Est. cost ESP32-CAM board (ESP32 + OV2640 camera + memory + built-in flash LED) $4.00 RS-485 adapter module (MAX485 class) $0.60 24 V → 3.3/5 V buck module (MP1584 class) $0.50 Wires, screw terminal, heat-shrink $0.40 3D-printed ASA shell, about 40 g $0.80 Clear window + gasket + small cable gland $0.50 Mounting: U-bolt or hose clamp + screws $0.60 Markers: 10-year-rated prismatic retroreflective sheeting, pink and yellow $0.40 20 cd LED + driver MOSFET for the 2 ms night flash $0.35 Lens hood and marker snow caps (printed with the shell) $0.20 Water-shedding window coating $0.05 Total ≈ $8.40

The extra items are what the Test Log showed it takes to work in every condition: night, rain, hail, snow, dust and 10 years of UV. Torsional dampers, if ARRAY adds them, are part of the tracker structure and not in this unit cost.

docs.title: What the margin buys
docs.text: About $1.60 is left under $10. That can cover price swings.

docs.title: Trade-offs of no PCB
docs.text:
• Faster start. Firmware work can begin right away with no board design or fabrication.
  • Heat rating. Cheap camera boards and modules usually aren't guaranteed for +60 °C, so test them before trusting them in the field.
  • Wiring. Hand-soldered joints can loosen with wind vibration. Use screw terminals and strain relief, and pot the connections.
  • Sponsor fit. ARRAY prefers UL/cULus-listed parts. Whether a module build is acceptable beyond prototypes needs confirming with ARRAY.

docs.title: Gazebo Model
docs.text:
The same setup as the browser simulation, built as a Gazebo world so the team can test the vision code against a full physics simulation on a laptop. Built by Lakshanand Sugumar.

Gazebo runs on your computer, not in a web page. The field simulation is the in-browser version.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
In the repository under simulation/gazebo/:

File What it is tilt_camera.sdf The world: drive row, follower row on a revolute joint, camera on a fixed post, pink and yellow markers, Arizona sun scripts/tilt_vision.py Color subtraction, marker centers and the taught-table estimator scripts/gz_tilt.py Teach, test and live modes that drive the follower joint and read the camera

docs.title: What's in the world
docs.text:
• Follower row 5.8 m from the camera, on a revolute joint about the row axis, limited to ±60°
  • Camera: 640 × 480, 60° horizontal view, 10 Hz, Gaussian noise, on a post 0.5 m above the tube
  • 10 cm markers: pink on the near edge, yellow on the far edge, 1 m apart along the row
  • Joint angle set over /follower/tilt_cmd, ground truth from the joint state topic

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Needs Gazebo Harmonic (gz-sim 8) with its Python bindings, and numpy. Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 is the easiest setup.

cd simulation/gazebo
gz sim -r tilt_camera.sdf

In a second terminal:

cd simulation/gazebo/scripts
python3 gz_tilt.py teach
python3 gz_tilt.py test --n 40

teach sweeps the follower from −60° to +60° in 2° steps and saves table.json. test tilts it to random angles and prints the error statistics.

Not yet run

These files were written to match the browser simulation but haven't been run in Gazebo yet. Expect to adjust joint gains or topic names on the first run.

docs.title: Test Log: Where the Markers Were Lost, and the Fixes
docs.text: A record of every failure the field simulation found, the cause, the fix, and the result before and after. Each test is 40 random follower angles between −55° and +55° unless noted, judged against the ±1° target. The loss sweeps step through every degree from −60° to +60°. Testing and fixes by Lakshanand Sugumar, November 2026.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: # Where it failed Cause Fix Before After 1 Every condition, follower at +5° to +14° Torque tube blocks the line of sight to the far marker Read the angle from the near marker when the far one is blocked 35–38 of 40 read 40 of 40, max 0.24° 2 Thunderstorm, rain Drops crossing the markers in most frames 7-frame median in rain, hail and snow 39/40 within ±1°, max 3.31° 40/40, max 0.55° 3 Snow Snow building up on the marker faces shifts their color unevenly 3D-printed snow caps over the markers 30/40 within ±1° 40/40, max 0.24° 4 UV aging Colors fade until the fixed threshold rejects them Noise-adaptive threshold, and 10-year-rated prismatic sheeting 0/40 at 10 years 40/40, max 0.51° 5 Night, no light Nothing to see Retroreflective sheeting with a 20 cd LED flash 0/40 40/40 all night 6 Night, row twisting in wind Long exposure blurs the moving markers 2 ms flash pulse, with the reference frame taken the same way 39/40, max 1.54° 40/40, max 0.49° 7 High wind, flat stow Torsional galloping: wind damping goes negative Torsional dampers on the follower damping −0.6% damping +7.2%

docs.title: 1. Torque tube blocks the far marker
docs.text:
Found by: the loss sweep, in every weather condition. The yellow marker on the far edge disappeared between about +5° and +14°.

Cause: at those angles the camera, the torque tube and the far marker line up, so the tube is in the way. I first tried moving the far marker onto a 25 cm arm past the module edge. The loss only moved to +4° to +12°. Any marker on the far side of the tube has to pass behind the tube at some angle, so no mounting position can avoid it.

Fix: the near pink marker is never behind the tube. When the far marker is blocked, the camera reads the angle from the near marker's position alone. The camera post moves only about 0.01° in wind, so the near marker alone is accurate.

Result: sweeps in clear, windy, rain, thunderstorm, hail, snow, dust storm and fog all had zero angles without a reading. Noon test: 40/40, max error 0.24°.

docs.title: 2. Rain and storm drops
docs.text:
Found by: the thunderstorm test. One reading was off by 3.31°.

Cause: in heavy rain, drops on the window and in the air cross the markers in most frames, which a 3-frame median can't reject.

Fix: a lens hood with a water-shedding window coating, plus an adaptive filter. The camera takes the median of 7 frames in rain, hail or snow, and 3 otherwise. The follower moves slowly, so the extra half-second costs nothing.

Result: thunderstorm 40/40 within ±1°, max 0.55°. Hail max 0.48°. Rain max 0.40°.

docs.title: 3. Snow on the markers
docs.text:
Found by: the snow test, with a steady bias of about 0.5° rather than random scatter.

Cause: snow building up on the markers changes the color of the lit and shaded faces by different amounts, which moves the blob's center.

Fix: small 3D-printed snow caps over each marker.

Result: without caps, 30/40 within ±1°. With caps, 40/40, max 0.24°.

docs.title: 4. UV fading
docs.text:
Found by: the aging tests. After 10 years, 0 of 40 readings.

Cause: faded markers still stand out from the noise, but the fixed color threshold rejected them.

Fix: the threshold now adapts to each image's own noise. It can drop below the old value for faded markers, but never rises above it, so rain clutter can't push it up. The marker material also matters:

Material Result Prismatic retroreflective sheeting, 10-year rated 40/40 at 10 years, max 0.51° Standard colored vinyl 24/38 within ±1° at 3 years, none found at 6 years Fluorescent vinyl tape 20/36 within ±1° at 6 months, none found at 1 year

Decision: use 10-year-rated prismatic sheeting.

docs.title: 5. Night
docs.text:
Found by: night tests. With no light, no readings.

Fix: retroreflective sheeting with a 20 cd LED flash on the drive row. The camera takes one frame with the flash and one without, then subtracts them. An 8 cd LED was marginal and 4 cd failed.

Result (Dec 21): 40/40 within ±1° at 17:45 (dusk), 18:30, 19:30 and 04:30 (pre-dawn). Max error 0.69°.

docs.title: Glow-in-the-dark markers (strontium aluminate)
docs.text:
Glow cores charge in sunlight and glow at night with no power. I modeled the afterglow fading as roughly t^−1.1, starting at 0.3 cd/m² ten minutes after sunset, and the camera stacking ten 2-second exposures.

Time after sunset Glow Result 52 min 49 mcd/m² All found, but readings biased about 2° (cause not yet found) 97 min 25 mcd/m² 40/40 within ±1°, max 0.69° 157 min 15 mcd/m² 0/40, even with 30 cm markers 11.6 h (pre-dawn) ~1 mcd/m² 0/40

Decision: glow markers can't cover the whole night with a camera this cheap, because the afterglow fades too far. The flash covers the whole night, so it's the primary night method. Glow stays in the simulation as an option.

docs.title: 6. Motion blur at night
docs.text:
Found by: markers 25 m from the drive point, in 12 m/s wind, at night. The row twists up to ±7° at 1.9 Hz.

Cause: a 1/15 s exposure blurs the moving markers. The flash's reference frame was also taken later than the lit frame.

Fix: a 2 ms flash pulse, with the reference frame taken with the same timing straight after.

Result: long exposure 39/40, max 1.54°. Pulse 40/40, max 0.49°. Pulse in a night thunderstorm: 40/40, max 0.55°.

docs.title: 7. Torsional galloping
docs.text:
Found by: watching the twist live in 19 m/s wind, with the rows in flat stow and the markers 25 m out.

Cause: near flat tilt, wind adds negative damping to the twist motion. At 19 m/s the total damping was −0.6%, so the twist grows on its own. It grows slowly at that speed, but the effect increases with wind speed.

Setup Total damping Largest twist in 12 s Flat stow −0.6% (galloping) 0.74°, growing 30° stow +3.0% 14.1° (steady wind torque at 30°) Flat stow + dampers +7.2% 3.7°

Decision: flat stow with torsional dampers. A 30° stow avoids galloping but takes a large steady twist with the assumed tube. This is ARRAY's structure, so the camera just measures it. Recommend raising it with ARRAY.

docs.title: Bugs found in the simulator itself
docs.text:
These were problems in my simulation code, not in the design:

  • Night was too bright. The night sky used an arbitrary light level. Replaced with measured twilight levels.
  • Brighter LED gave worse results. Flash frames used a fixed exposure, so markers clipped to white. Fixed by setting the exposure from the expected return.
  • Glow was invisible. The 16-bit image buffer rounded very dim light to zero. Fixed with a 32-bit float buffer.
  • Noise model was too crude. Replaced with a physical model in electrons (read noise, shot noise, dark current).
  • Image rounded before noise. Sub-DN signals vanished before stacking could recover them. Fixed by adding noise before 8-bit rounding, as a real sensor does.
  • Mismatched reference. The test compared a median of frames against an average of true angles. Fixed by keeping the median frame together with its own true angle.

docs.title: What it found about the tracker itself
docs.text:
• Wind twist: with the assumed tube, the follower 25 m from the drive point twists up to about 6° at 12 m/s and about 9° at 19 m/s. Markers at the drive point measure linkage misalignment alone. Markers near the row end also see wind twist.
  • Torsional galloping: in flat stow above about 18 m/s the twist damping turns negative. Torsional dampers fix it. A 30° stow avoids it but takes a large steady twist. This is ARRAY's structure, so raise it with ARRAY.

These numbers depend on assumed row and tube sizes. Swap in ARRAY's values when they arrive.

docs.title: Field Simulation
docs.text:
A physics-based model of the field near Phoenix, covering: - Sun and light: the real sun path and daylight, twilight and night light levels - Weather: rain, thunderstorms, hail, snow, dust storms and fog - Structure: gusting wind that twists the torque tube, including torsional galloping, and drive-linkage backlash - Optics: a real lens with distortion, and UV fading of the markers - Sensor: a camera with real exposure limits and noise

It runs in your browser. Built by Lakshanand Sugumar.

Open full screen

docs.title: Try this
docs.text:
1. Press Teach at midday. This is the on-site calibration sweep against a reference inclinometer.
  2. Press Run 40-angle test to see the accuracy, or Find marker losses to sweep every degree and list where a marker goes missing and why.
  3. Pick a Weather condition, then turn the Fixes off one at a time to see what each one does.
  4. Move Markers and camera along the row toward the row end, raise the wind, and watch the tube twist.
  5. Slide past sunset. The flash keeps it working all night. Try the glow-in-the-dark cores instead and watch them fade.

docs.title: The physics
docs.text:
Part Model Sun Solar position for 33.4° N. Direct beam through the Kasten–Young air mass, about 105 lm/W. Clear-sky diffuse light and published twilight levels down to 0.0007 lx Clouds Overcast cuts the direct beam and scales the diffuse light for each weather type Visibility Koschmieder extinction, σ = 3.912 / visibility. Rain adds σ ≈ 0.21 R^0.74 per km Rain, snow, hail Falling at real speeds and drifting with the wind. Hail falls at its terminal velocity with impact energy shown. Drops and flakes on the window refract and blur the image Tracking True tracking with backtracking. Generic stow rules: hail and snow to 60°, wind above 17 m/s to 30° or flat Wind Gusts with 20% turbulence intensity and a 25 m length scale. Torque = ½ρU² · CM(tilt) · chord² Tube twist Steel torsion, first mode about 1.9 Hz, 3% damping. Galloping is modeled as negative aerodynamic damping near flat tilt Drive linkage A backlash deadband that flips side when the torque reverses, plus elastic wind-up Camera post 2 in. schedule-40 steel pipe bending under wind drag Lens Barrel distortion with k₁ adjustable Sensor 640 × 480. Auto exposure from 1/8000 s to 1/15 s, then gain to 16×. Read noise, shot noise and dark current in electrons, with dark current doubling every 6.5 °C. Rounded to 8 bits after the noise Sensor heat Enclosure temperature from the air and the sun. Warns above the OV2640's 50 °C stable-image and 70 °C operating limits Night flash Retroreflected luminance = RA × LED intensity ÷ distance². Flash frames can be 2 ms pulses Glow cores Strontium aluminate afterglow decaying as t^−1.1. Night stacking of ten 2 s exposures UV aging Color fades exponentially with years in the field, at a different rate for each marker material

Assumed values, not from ARRAY

ARRAY hasn't given row dimensions, tube size, stow angles or wind data yet, so these are assumptions: 60 m rows driven at the middle, a 127 mm square tube with 3.5 mm wall, 28 kg modules, a hinge-moment peak of CM = 0.13, galloping onset near 18 m/s, and linkage stiffness of 1.5 MN·m/rad. Fade rates, glow brightness and sensor noise are representative values, not measurements. Swap in real numbers when they arrive.

The camera reports the angle to the ARRAY controller over RS-485. ARRAY hasn't specified the controller's message format yet, so the simulation shows only the angle.
